frame.objective: Determine whether Jotun should invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case leveraging its marine and protective coatings technology, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to mid-2024; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12-week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies investment, not just theoretical potential.
Must consider Jotun’s existing B2B focus and current consumer reach (unknown).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., DIY marine boat maintenance, residential protective coatings for decks/fences).
2) Expand consumer reach without differentiation (e.g., sell existing marine/protective coatings through retail channels, online marketplace).
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on B2B shipyards, ship owners, infrastructure, and industry customers.
4) License marine/protective coating technology to third-party consumer brands for co-branded products.

T1.claim: DIY boat owners will purchase marine coatings if they perceive them as a necessary maintenance item for protecting their investment, and Jotun can capture value by selling through its existing Multicolor Center network at premium prices.
T1.who_benefits: Jotun benefits from higher-margin direct-to-consumer sales and increased brand visibility among boat owners.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Boat owners treat marine coatings as essential for preventing corrosion and maintaining vessel value; they are willing to pay more for professional-grade products they trust.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Jotun sells through its 10,000+ Multicolor machines and centers, capturing retail margins and building consumer brand loyalty that can be leveraged for other product categories.
assumptions: Boat owners have sufficient disposable income to purchase premium marine coatings.
Jotun's marine coatings are perceived as superior to generic alternatives.
The Multicolor Center network can be effectively utilized to reach DIY boat owners.
predictions: If Jotun launches a targeted consumer proposition for marine coatings, sales through Multicolor Centers will increase by at least 10% within 12 weeks.
Customer surveys will show that at least 60% of DIY boat owners consider marine coatings a necessary expense rather than optional.
T1.first_claim: DIY boat owners will purchase marine coatings if they perceive them as a necessary maintenance item for protecting their investment, and Jotun can capture value by selling through its existing Multicolor Center network at premium prices.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt marine coatings as a fashion or lifestyle accessory if they view them as a way to express personal style and status, leading to multiple purchases per boat owner.
T2.who_benefits: Jotun benefits from higher volume sales and premium pricing for designer colors and finishes.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Boat owners increasingly treat vessels as personal expression platforms; they seek unique colors and finishes to differentiate their boats and signal status.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Jotun can introduce limited-edition color palettes and co-branded finishes, selling through its retail network at premium prices, capturing both product and design value.
assumptions: Boat owners are willing to spend on aesthetic enhancements beyond functional protection.
Jotun can develop distinctive color systems that resonate with consumer trends.
The retail network can effectively showcase and sell fashion-oriented marine coatings.
predictions: If Jotun launches a fashion-focused marine coating line, repeat purchase rate among DIY boat owners will exceed 20% within 12 weeks.
Social media engagement (shares, follows) for the new color line will be at least 1.5x higher than for standard marine coatings.
T2.first_claim: Consumers will adopt marine coatings as a fashion or lifestyle accessory if they view them as a way to express personal style and status, leading to multiple purchases per boat owner.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs Generic Marine Coatings
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are shown two product descriptions: (1) Jotun Marine Pro – premium protective coating marketed as essential for boat maintenance; (2) Generic Marine Coating – basic protective coating marketed as affordable alternative. They are asked to indicate likelihood to purchase (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay. A
X1.sample: 200 DIY boat owners recruited via marine forums and social media, balanced by boat size and experience level.
X1.measure: Average purchase likelihood score for premium product vs generic product; maximum price willingness to pay for each.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium product will have at least 15 points higher purchase likelihood score and a 20% higher maximum price willingness to pay than generic product.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Premium product will have at most 5 points higher purchase likelihood score and no significant difference in maximum price willingness to pay compared to generic product.

X1.decision_rule: If premium product’s purchase likelihood score exceeds generic by ≥ 15 points AND its maximum price willingness is at least 20% higher, proceed with consumer proposition development. Otherwise, reject.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-D) is about warehouse packing errors and label printers, which is unrelated to consumer behavior, marine coatings demand, or DIY boat owners. It bears no relevance to T1 or T2.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence base is insufficient to support either theory as likely. T1 (functional necessity) is more plausible than T2 (fashion/lifestyle) given the nature of marine coatings as protective materials, but no real source supports it. Proceed with the proposed consumer preference test (X1) before committing to development.
final.target_customer: DIY boat owners who maintain their own vessels
final.value_proposition: Premium protective marine coatings positioned as essential maintenance for preserving vessel value
final.next_action: Execute the consumer preference test (X1) to validate willingness to pay for premium marine coatings before investing in product development.
final.uncertainty: High - no real evidence supports either theory; the test is the only way to reduce uncertainty.
would_change_if: The test shows premium product has at least 15 points higher purchase likelihood and 20% higher price willingness than generic

position.recommendation: Proceed with the proposed consumer preference test (X1) before committing to a differentiated consumer proposition. The evidence base is insufficient to support either theory as likely, but T1 (functional necessity) is more plausible than T2 (fashion/lifestyle) given the nature of marine coatings as protective materials. The test will determine if DIY boat owners value premium protection enough to pay a premium price

frame.objective: Determine whether Jotun should invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case leveraging its marine and protective coatings technology, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to mid-2024; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12-week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies investment, not just theoretical potential.
Must consider Jotun’s existing B2B focus and current consumer reach (unknown).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., DIY marine boat maintenance, residential protective coatings for decks/fences).
2) Expand consumer reach without differentiation (e.g., sell existing marine/protective coatings through retail channels, online marketplace).
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on B2B shipyards, ship owners, infrastructure, and industry customers.
4) License marine/protective coating technology to third-party consumer brands for co-branded products.

T1.claim: DIY boat owners will purchase marine coatings if they perceive them as a necessary maintenance item for protecting their investment, and Jotun can capture value by selling through its existing Multicolor Center network at premium prices.
T1.who_benefits: Jotun benefits from higher-margin direct-to-consumer sales and increased brand visibility among boat owners.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Boat owners treat marine coatings as essential for preventing corrosion and maintaining vessel value; they are willing to pay more for professional-grade products they trust.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Jotun sells through its 10,000+ Multicolor machines and centers, capturing retail margins and building consumer brand loyalty that can be leveraged for other product categories.
assumptions: Boat owners have sufficient disposable income to purchase premium marine coatings.
Jotun's marine coatings are perceived as superior to generic alternatives.
The Multicolor Center network can be effectively utilized to reach DIY boat owners.
predictions: If Jotun launches a targeted consumer proposition for marine coatings, sales through Multicolor Centers will increase by at least 10% within 12 weeks.
Customer surveys will show that at least 60% of DIY boat owners consider marine coatings a necessary expense rather than optional.
T1.first_claim: DIY boat owners will purchase marine coatings if they perceive them as a necessary maintenance item for protecting their investment, and Jotun can capture value by selling through its existing Multicolor Center network at premium prices.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt marine coatings as a fashion or lifestyle accessory if they view them as a way to express personal style and status, leading to multiple purchases per boat owner.
T2.who_benefits: Jotun benefits from higher volume sales and premium pricing for designer colors and finishes.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Boat owners increasingly treat vessels as personal expression platforms; they seek unique colors and finishes to differentiate their boats and signal status.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Jotun can introduce limited-edition color palettes and co-branded finishes, selling through its retail network at premium prices, capturing both product and design value.
assumptions: Boat owners are willing to spend on aesthetic enhancements beyond functional protection.
Jotun can develop distinctive color systems that resonate with consumer trends.
The retail network can effectively showcase and sell fashion-oriented marine coatings.
predictions: If Jotun launches a fashion-focused marine coating line, repeat purchase rate among DIY boat owners will exceed 20% within 12 weeks.
Social media engagement (shares, follows) for the new color line will be at least 1.5x higher than for standard marine coatings.
T2.first_claim: Consumers will adopt marine coatings as a fashion or lifestyle accessory if they view them as a way to express personal style and status, leading to multiple purchases per boat owner.

assessments.quote: A leader in marine coatings for the new-build, dry-dock, tank and cargo holds, and sea-stock markets, the Marine Coatings business also provides coatings for mega-yachts and leisure yachts.
assessments.does_not_show: The source does not address consumer demand, DIY boat owners, or willingness to pay premium prices for maintenance coatings.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs Generic Marine Coatings
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are shown two product descriptions: (1) Jotun Marine Pro – premium protective coating marketed as essential for boat maintenance; (2) Generic Marine Coating – basic protective coating marketed as affordable alternative. They are asked to indicate likelihood to purchase (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay. A
X1.sample: 200 DIY boat owners recruited via marine forums and social media, balanced by boat size and experience level.
X1.measure: Average purchase likelihood score for premium product vs generic product; maximum price willingness to pay for each.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium product will have at least 15 points higher purchase likelihood score and a 20% higher maximum price willingness to pay than generic product.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Premium product will have at most 5 points higher purchase likelihood score and no significant difference in maximum price willingness to pay compared to generic product.

X1.decision_rule: If premium product’s purchase likelihood score exceeds generic by ≥ 15 points AND its maximum price willingness is at least 20% higher, proceed with consumer proposition development. Otherwise, reject.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-D) is about warehouse packing errors and label printers, which is unrelated to consumer behavior, marine coatings demand, or DIY boat owners. It bears no relevance to T1 or T2.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence base is insufficient to support either theory as likely. T1 (functional necessity) is more plausible than T2 (fashion/lifestyle) given the nature of marine coatings as protective materials, but no real source supports it. Proceed with the proposed consumer preference test (X1) before committing to development.
final.target_customer: DIY boat owners who maintain their own vessels
final.value_proposition: Premium protective marine coatings positioned as essential maintenance for preserving vessel value
final.next_action: Execute the consumer preference test (X1) to validate willingness to pay for premium marine coatings before investing in product development.
final.uncertainty: High - no real evidence supports either theory; the test is the only way to reduce uncertainty.
would_change_if: The test shows premium product has at least 15 points higher purchase likelihood and 20% higher price willingness than generic

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in 1993 to justify Tanita investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser currently used in clinics and health clubs.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; cannot use later developments or internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to individual buyers.
Must consider alternatives including no expansion, different customer groups, or different product routes.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual consumers for home use (e.g., personal body‑fat monitoring).
2) Expand the existing stand‑on analyser to new B2B segments such as corporate wellness programs, gyms, or insurance providers.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current clinic and health‑club markets without new consumer offering.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products.
5) Create a subscription or service model for ongoing body‑fat tracking and health insights.

T1.claim: Individual consumers will adopt a home body‑fat analyser if they view it as a medical necessity for health monitoring, leading them to purchase the device directly.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking health monitoring; Tanita benefits from direct sales and premium pricing.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing public awareness of obesity‑related diseases (e.g., heart disease, diabetes) creates demand for at‑home health tools.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita sells the device through retail channels at a price above cost, capturing margin on each unit.
assumptions: Consumers trust bioelectrical impedance as a reliable health metric.
Retail distribution is feasible and can reach target consumers.
Price sensitivity is low enough for a premium device.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase a home body‑fat analyser.
Sales data (if available) will show a measurable share of units sold to individuals rather than institutions.
T1.first_claim: Individual consumers will adopt a home body‑fat analyser if they view it as a medical necessity for health monitoring, leading them to purchase the device directly.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a home body‑fat analyser primarily as a fashion or lifestyle accessory, leading them to purchase multiple devices for different outfits or social contexts.
T2.who_benefits: Consumers seeking self‑expression and social signaling; Tanita benefits from higher volume sales and potential accessory add‑ons.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Cultural trends in the 1990s emphasize personal style and visible health metrics as status symbols.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita captures value through higher unit volume and optional accessories (e.g., interchangeable covers, data‑logging services).
assumptions: Fashion cycles drive demand for multiple devices.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for aesthetic differentiation.
Retail partners will stock multiple variants.
predictions: Consumers will report owning more than one body‑fat analyser.
Sales data will show a higher proportion of repeat purchases compared to a single‑purchase medical‑necessity model.

final.target_customer: Individual consumers seeking health monitoring (T1) or lifestyle expression (T2)

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in 1993 to justify Tanita investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser currently used in clinics and health clubs.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; cannot use later developments or internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to individual buyers.
Must consider alternatives including no expansion, different customer groups, or different product routes.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual consumers for home use (e.g., personal body‑fat monitoring).
2) Expand the existing stand‑on analyser to new B2B segments such as corporate wellness programs, gyms, or insurance providers.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current clinic and health‑club markets without new consumer offering.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products.
5) Create a subscription or service model for ongoing body‑fat tracking and health insights.

T1.claim: Individual consumers will adopt a home body‑fat analyser if they view it as a medical necessity for health monitoring, leading them to purchase the device directly.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking health monitoring; Tanita benefits from direct sales and premium pricing.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing public awareness of obesity‑related diseases (e.g., heart disease, diabetes) creates demand for at‑home health tools.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita sells the device through retail channels at a price above cost, capturing margin on each unit.
assumptions: Consumers trust bioelectrical impedance as a reliable health metric.
Retail distribution is feasible and can reach target consumers.
Price sensitivity is low enough for a premium device.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase a home body‑fat analyser.
Sales data (if available) will show a measurable share of units sold to individuals rather than institutions.
T1.first_claim: Individual consumers will adopt a home body‑fat analyser if they view it as a medical necessity for health monitoring, leading them to purchase the device directly.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a home body‑fat analyser primarily as a fashion or lifestyle accessory, leading them to purchase multiple devices for different outfits or social contexts.
T2.who_benefits: Consumers seeking self‑expression and social signaling; Tanita benefits from higher volume sales and potential accessory add‑ons.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Cultural trends in the 1990s emphasize personal style and visible health metrics as status symbols.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita captures value through higher unit volume and optional accessories (e.g., interchangeable covers, data‑logging services).
assumptions: Fashion cycles drive demand for multiple devices.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for aesthetic differentiation.
Retail partners will stock multiple variants.
predictions: Consumers will report owning more than one body‑fat analyser.
Sales data will show a higher proportion of repeat purchases compared to a single‑purchase medical‑necessity model.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002
No internal company data available
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment
Must consider alternatives including no expansion
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual outdoor enthusiasts (e.g., hikers, sailors) with a dedicated 406 MHz beacon product
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into new commercial segments (e.g., recreational marine, aviation hobbyists) without a differentiated consumer proposition
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current ship and aircraft emergency beacon and military/commercial marine survival light markets
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications
5) Form a partnership with outdoor recreation brands to co‑brand a consumer beacon product

T1.claim: Regulatory approval and mandatory registration create a clear, legally required market for 406 MHz PLBs among individual outdoor users, driving purchase decisions.
T1.who_benefits: Outdoor enthusiasts who need a reliable distress beacon for remote activities; ACR Electronics benefits by capturing sales of approved devices.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The FCC rule change (2002) made 406 MHz PLBs the only legally recognized distress beacon for land-based emergencies, removing uncertainty and creating a compliance-driven purchase requirement.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can price at premium levels (e.g., $700) and sell through existing distribution channels, capturing value from the regulatory mandate.
assumptions: Regulatory approval is a primary driver of consumer adoption
Outdoor users prioritize compliance and reliability over price
ACR's existing distribution can reach individual buyers
predictions: If a competitor launches a non‑406 MHz beacon, it will not be adopted by users seeking compliance
Sales of ACR's GyPSI 406 will correlate with regions where the rule is enforced
Consumer surveys will show that regulatory approval is a top reason for purchase
T1.first_claim: Regulatory approval and mandatory registration create a clear, legally required market for 406 MHz PLBs among individual outdoor users, driving purchase decisions.

T2.claim: Outdoor recreation culture and peer influence create demand for PLBs as safety gear, independent of regulatory mandates.
T2.who_benefits: Outdoor enthusiasts who value safety and community norms; ACR Electronics benefits by selling through outdoor retailers and leveraging brand reputation.

T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can partner with outdoor brands, sell through specialty retailers, and command premium pricing based on perceived safety value.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates are rising

predictions: In regions with high outdoor participation, PLB sales will be higher even without regulatory mandates

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002
No internal company data available
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment
Must consider alternatives including no expansion
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual outdoor enthusiasts (e.g., hikers, sailors) with a dedicated 406 MHz beacon product
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into new commercial segments (e.g., recreational marine, aviation hobbyists) without a differentiated consumer proposition
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current ship and aircraft emergency beacon and military/commercial marine survival light markets
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications
5) Form a partnership with outdoor recreation brands to co‑brand a consumer beacon product

T1.claim: Regulatory approval and mandatory registration create a clear, legally required market for 406 MHz PLBs among individual outdoor users, driving purchase decisions.
T1.who_benefits: Outdoor enthusiasts who need a reliable distress beacon for remote activities; ACR Electronics benefits by capturing sales of approved devices.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The FCC rule change (2002) made 406 MHz PLBs the only legally recognized distress beacon for land-based emergencies, removing uncertainty and creating a compliance-driven purchase requirement.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can price at premium levels (e.g., $700) and sell through existing distribution channels, capturing value from the regulatory mandate.
assumptions: Regulatory approval is a primary driver of consumer adoption
Outdoor users prioritize compliance and reliability over price
ACR's existing distribution can reach individual buyers
predictions: If a competitor launches a non‑406 MHz beacon, it will not be adopted by users seeking compliance
Sales of ACR's GyPSI 406 will correlate with regions where the rule is enforced
Consumer surveys will show that regulatory approval is a top reason for purchase
T1.first_claim: Regulatory approval and mandatory registration create a clear, legally required market for 406 MHz PLBs among individual outdoor users, driving purchase decisions.

T2.claim: Outdoor recreation culture and peer influence create demand for PLBs as safety gear, independent of regulatory mandates.

T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can partner with outdoor brands, sell through specialty retailers, and command premium pricing based on perceived safety value.

Peer influence and safety culture drive purchase decisions
ACR's brand is trusted by outdoor communities
predictions: In regions with high outdoor participation, PLB sales will be higher even without regulatory mandates

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002
No internal company data available
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment
Must consider alternatives including no expansion
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual outdoor enthusiasts (e.g., hikers, sailors) with a dedicated 406 MHz beacon product
2) Expand the existing B2B product line into new commercial segments (e.g., recreational marine, aviation hobbyists) without a differentiated consumer proposition
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current ship and aircraft emergency beacon and military/commercial marine survival light markets
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications
5) Form a partnership with outdoor recreation brands to co‑brand a consumer beacon product

T1.claim: Regulatory approval and mandatory registration create a clear, legally required market for 406 MHz PLBs among individual outdoor users, driving purchase decisions.
T1.who_benefits: Outdoor enthusiasts who need a reliable distress beacon for remote activities; ACR Electronics benefits by capturing sales of approved devices.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The FCC rule change (2002) made 406 MHz PLBs the only legally recognized distress beacon for land-based emergencies, removing uncertainty and creating a compliance-driven purchase requirement.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can price at premium levels (e.g., $700) and sell through existing distribution channels, capturing value from the regulatory mandate.
assumptions: Regulatory approval is a primary driver of consumer adoption
Outdoor users prioritize compliance and reliability over price
ACR's existing distribution can reach individual buyers
predictions: If a competitor launches a non‑406 MHz beacon, it will not be adopted by users seeking compliance
Sales of ACR's GyPSI 406 will correlate with regions where the rule is enforced
Consumer surveys will show that regulatory approval is a top reason for purchase

Peer influence and safety culture drive purchase decisions
ACR's brand is trusted by outdoor communities

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources available before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12-week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and feasibility of adapting tractor technology for individual buyers.
Consider existing dealer network and current product portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small farm, hobbyist, or residential) using Deere's tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers more directly, without creating a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B agricultural and industrial equipment sales.
4) License Deere's tractor technology to third-party manufacturers for consumer applications.

T1.claim: Households with small gardens adopt lawn tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for multiple chores, and economical to maintain.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners with small gardens who need efficient yard maintenance.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They perceive lawn tractors as cost-effective and versatile tools that reduce manual labor, making them attractive compared to traditional methods.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can capture value by selling lawn tractors through its existing dealer network at premium prices, leveraging brand reputation and economies of scale.
assumptions: Small garden households represent a sizable market segment in the 1960s.
Price sensitivity is a key driver for this segment.
Deere's dealer network can effectively reach these consumers.
predictions: If Deere introduces a lawn tractor priced competitively, sales among small garden households will increase.
Surveyed homeowners will rank cost-effectiveness and versatility as top purchase criteria.

assumptions: Suburban population growth in the 1960s created a new consumer segment.
Brand trust is a significant factor in purchase decisions for durable goods.
Deere's dealer network can be adapted to serve suburban consumers.
predictions: In areas with high suburban growth, lawn tractor adoption rates will be higher.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources available before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12-week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and feasibility of adapting tractor technology for individual buyers.
Consider existing dealer network and current product portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small farm, hobbyist, or residential) using Deere's tractor engineering.

T1.claim: Households with small gardens adopt lawn tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for multiple chores, and economical to maintain.

assumptions: Small garden households represent a sizable market segment in the 1960s.
Price sensitivity is a key driver for this segment.
Deere's dealer network can effectively reach these consumers.
predictions: If Deere introduces a lawn tractor priced competitively, sales among small garden households will increase.
Surveyed homeowners will rank cost-effectiveness and versatility as top purchase criteria.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources available before mid-1962; no internal company data.

Must identify evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and feasibility of adapting tractor technology for individual buyers.
Consider existing dealer network and current product portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small farm, hobbyist, or residential) using Deere's tractor engineering.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources available before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12-week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and feasibility of adapting tractor technology for individual buyers.
Consider existing dealer network and current product portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small farm, hobbyist, or residential) using Deere's tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers more directly, without creating a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B agricultural and industrial equipment sales.
4) License Deere's tractor technology to third-party manufacturers for consumer applications.

T1.claim: Households with small gardens adopt lawn tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for multiple chores, and economical to maintain.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners with small gardens who need efficient yard maintenance.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They perceive lawn tractors as cost-effective and versatile tools that reduce manual labor, making them attractive compared to traditional methods.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can capture value by selling lawn tractors through its existing dealer network at premium prices, leveraging brand reputation and economies of scale.
assumptions: Small garden households represent a sizable market segment in the 1960s.
Price sensitivity is a key driver for this segment.
Deere's dealer network can effectively reach these consumers.
predictions: If Deere introduces a lawn tractor priced competitively, sales among small garden households will increase.
Surveyed homeowners will rank cost-effectiveness and versatility as top purchase criteria.
T1.first_claim: Households with small gardens adopt lawn tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for multiple chores, and economical to maintain.

T2.claim: Homeowners adopt lawn tractors because suburban expansion creates a need for mechanized yard care, and Deere's brand reputation for reliability makes it a trusted choice.
T2.who_benefits: Suburban homeowners who lack time or physical ability for manual yard work.

T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere can capture value by leveraging its brand to command premium pricing and by expanding its dealer network to serve suburban markets.
assumptions: Suburban population growth in the 1960s created a new consumer segment.
Brand trust is a significant factor in purchase decisions for durable goods.
Deere's dealer network can be adapted to serve suburban consumers.
predictions: In areas with high suburban growth, lawn tractor adoption rates will be higher.
